title: Known Completely, Found Everywhere
overview: The poet marvels that God knows them through and through, is present everywhere and shaped them before birth, then turns to anger at God's enemies and asks to be examined.

parts.label: God knows every move (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: The poet speaks straight to God, saying God knows their resting, rising and thoughts, and even their words before they are spoken. Being surrounded and touched by God's hand could feel either protective or confining, and the poet simply calls such knowledge too great to grasp.

parts.label: No place to hide (vv. 7-12)
parts.note: The poet imagines fleeing to the sky, to the realm of the dead (called Sheol in Hebrew), to the farthest sea, or into darkness, and finds God already there. Readers differ on whether this is mainly comfort or an admission that escape is impossible, and the poem seems to hold both, since God's hand both guides and holds fast.

parts.label: Shaped before birth (vv. 13-18)
parts.note: The poet pictures God weaving them together in the womb, poetically called the depths of the earth because it is hidden from sight. The book where their days were written is a poetic image, and readers differ on whether it means God simply knows a life ahead of time or plans it.

parts.label: Anger at God's enemies (vv. 19-22)
parts.note: The tone shifts sharply as the poet speaks of God slaying the wicked, which translations render either as a wish or as a confident statement, and declares open hatred for those who oppose God. It is a raw, uncomfortable outburst, and the psalm does not soften it.

parts.label: Search me too (vv. 23-24)
parts.note: The poet ends by turning the opening words into a request, asking God to examine their own heart and thoughts and lead them on the lasting way. Many read this as the poet checking that their anger against others has not hidden their own faults.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the harsh words against enemies in verses 19 to 22 are a fitting stance toward evil or an honest human cry that Jesus' teaching to love enemies later moves beyond.
think: Does the idea of being completely known by someone feel more like comfort or more like exposure to you, and why?
